text:
Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for evaluating this 18-year-old young man, whom I have followed alongside his family. His history is notable for recurrent, unexplained febrile episodes that first began around age 11. On examination, he has short stature with height well under the third percentile, mild baseline intellectual disability, and noticeable lateral webbing of his neck. His cardiopulmonary exam is completely normal, with clear breath sounds and regular heart sounds.

During his flares, we have documented diffuse cervical and inguinal nodal enlargement alongside a palpable liver edge and an enlarged spleen. Laboratory evaluation revealed acute hepatic inflammation with high serum ALT, AST, and GGT. His blood counts demonstrated severe anemia and thrombocytopenia, accompanied by a profound leukopenia characterized by marked depressions in absolute neutrophil, lymphocyte, and monocyte counts. Coagulation studies showed low fibrinogen, while fasting triglycerides and serum ferritin were both remarkably high. Further immunologic testing revealed an elevated soluble CD25 level and prominent surges in circulating interleukin-18, interleukin-1-beta, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Peripheral flow cytometry showed an expanded naive B-cell compartment; however, natural killer cell target lytic killing function was entirely normal. A subsequent bone marrow biopsy demonstrated clear hemophagocytic activity with histiocytes actively engulfing hematopoietic precursors.

He currently lives at home with his parents, attends a supported day program, and has no family history of hematologic or autoimmune conditions. He takes occasional paracetamol for symptomatic discomfort. 

Given this constellation of systemic inflammatory flares, cytopenias, and physical features, I would be grateful for your comprehensive assessment and recommendations.

Sincerely,
Dr. Julian Ross
